newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein to meet British officials in Belfast.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein to meet British officials in Belfast.

text.p: Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army, is expected to meet British officials on Wednesday for the first time since IRA guerrillas ended their truce last year, political sources said on Tuesday.

They said Sinn Fein politicians and civil servants planned to hold talks in Belfast after new British Prime Minister Tony Blair eased a ban on contacts in a bid to galvanise a paralysed three- year peace process.
Blair said he was prepared to allow officials talk with Sinn Fein to see whether the party and its IRA allies were ready to follow a peaceful path to win a voice in full talks.

He was adamant that a formal IRA ceasefire must be declared for Sinn Fein to be admitted to round-table talks involving Britain, Ireland and the rest of the province's bitterly divided Protestant and Roman Catholic parties.

Sinn Fein's delegation was likely to be led by Martin McGuinness, its chief negotiator who won seats in the British parliament along with party president Gerry Adams in May 1 elections that swept Blair's Labour Party to power.

Later this week Britain's new Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, will briefly visit Washington for discussions with U.S. government officials about peace hopes that have been shrouded in gloom since the IRA relaunched hostilities in 1996.
The IRA has waged a guerrilla campaign since 1969 to end British rule in Northern Ireland and unite it with Ireland.
Northern Ireland's 60 percent Protestant majority want to stay British but the 40 percent Roman Catholics, some of whom support the IRA, want a united Ireland freed of London's influence.
Adams challenged Britain on Tuesday to give a cast-iron guarantee of direct entry to peace talks for Sinn Fein if the IRA abandons violence.
Adams told the nationalist Irish News daily that if Britain gave clear assurances about viable all-party negotiations, Northern Ireland's floundering peace process could be restored.

In a direct response to Blair's speech, Adams said Britain "should state clearly that Sinn Fein will join the negotiations immediately following an unequivocal restoration of the IRA (Irish Republican Army) cessation of August 1994".
Blair gave a stern last-chance warning to Sinn Fein and the IRA to demonstrate a "words and deeds" commitment to peaceful methods to gain a voice in peace talks.
Adams criticised Blair for strongly defending Northern Ireland's union with Britain but also signalled his belief that any fresh IRA ceasefire would be unequivocal.
He said Blair's speech was "barren of new thinking" and that "nationalists felt disturbed to hear Mr Blair declare himself a unionist with such gusto."
Blair pledged that the province would remain under London while a majority supported it.
